Back is a Chinese FMV visual novel with pretty Asian girls, a bad English translation, and almost non-existent gameplay. First, I have to say a few good things about this “game” — the girls are genuinely cute, there are one or two decent jumpscare moments, and the few practical effects do the job. For a small indie studio — kudos. But the story is dull, many of the choices (which either are correct and let you progress, or wrong and force you to replay the scene) come without any explanation, or the explanation is completely lost in the incredibly poor translation. Gameplay elements are practically absent — after several minutes of watching videos, you get to choose between two or three options, of which only one is correct. No mysteries, no puzzles, nothing. Overall, a pretty disappointing product that I’m not even sure I can call a “game.” Video: [URL]

As well as two new tutorials and the challenges, we now have the possibility of random MOB events in Live Sailing, with the added complexity of random engine failure. Living with that prospect as you sail around adds a nice new element to things. I already felt like I had a working little yacht full of kit - charts and fenders and pencils and winch handles, plus a hand compass added recently - and now I've got the fender and bucket, a boat hook, I can chuck that horseshoe lifebelt off the back at last, and I've got more buttons to press - plus more things to tell my slow-moving crew to get on and do slowly. I do think we need a SHOUT AT THE CREW button to speed them up, especially when Bob the MOB is slowly sinking as his wellies fill with seawater, while the crew plod around, looking for a boat hook. Having the tutorials added to everything that eSail already teaches you is also great, adding more value to everything that's packed into eSail. I'll be honest, I'd rather see more serious stuff like this, than some of the other less realistic elements (dinosaur on a beach, I'm looking at you). This is a great add-on for eSail. I'm happy to support the devs as they keep building the base product and squashing bugs. They're communicative, supportive and approachable, so I was always going to go for this anyway. But, yes, I think that the extra depth this DLC adds to what you can do in the world is well worth the price tag.

After compelteing 100% of F1 manager 2024, would I recommend it? Disappointingly no. Now dont get me wrong this game has its positives, to start with it looks and sounds fantastic. Being not only fully licensed letting the real world of F1 be shown it also has audio snippets from the real drivers and crew members that give the game that little bit of life. On top of that although the game had a rough launch it has since been updated and made a stable and rather bug free experience. But unfortunately that doesn't distract from what I feel is poor gameplay. In terms of mid race planning and management the game is fine, the choices you make are no different that the other motorsport games you can pick up and play, however outside the racing I feel that there is too much of a focus on its real world comparisons and metrics rather than the gameplay being fun and understandable. There are so many systems that are too focused on accuracy that it takes away from the games feel. What I mean is shown in areas such as the part development where the game tends to show the specific metrics and how they are measured rather than just showing how it would affect the car and I feel this is a case of detail getting in the way of a game just being fun. The trend of the game being extremely detail oriented wouldn't be a issue if the game itself warranted it, but it forces you to learn and adjust to all the nitty gritty details of a F1 car and team and then the game itself is extremely easy to beat even when set to be realistic. Team fluctuate in performance way too much way too quickly, drivers make nonsensical moves and your targets are either way to easy to achieve or it's impossible to keep your job with again little to no sense being made by why they are the way they are. This is a type of game im quite familiar with having played hundreds of hours of motorsport manager, and having 100%'ed the previous 2 F1 manager games which I'm not reviewing retrospectively due to them having the same issue as this one does. And due to myself really enjoying management styled games I was wanting something I could sink my teeth into and waste hours upon hours playing and I just couldn't gel with it. Its as if its trying to be compared to the football manager series of games but with just surface level detail and no depth to what it means. and that makes the gameplay loop unsatisfying to be a part of. Motorsport manager has a less detailed and less impressive look and feel to the graphics and audio, it lacks the licencing meaning they use rip-off named parodies of the teams and drivers, and bends the rules to include mechanics such as promotion and demotion between the leagues of racing, so its far from a simulation of the F1 world, but its so much more fun as a game, which to me is more important. It has the depth of a true management game while still keeping the simplicity to help people who are not F1 mad adjust to the game. As a completionist the game has the expected challenges such as winning the championships, winning certain types of races, performing the general actions such as signing a driver as well as some more specific challenges such as having one of your drivers become the youngest world champion, winning all three championships at once (Driver, team and pit stop) and getting both drivers to a 100% setup at any race weekend. At launch some of these were bugged and unable to be obtained but to my knowledge these issues have been fixed. Its not really a impressive game to hunt, and depending on how much you focus just playing it for the certain achievements it also might end up being a rather large time sink and a boring one too as you might have won multiple championships but need to keep changing drivers while still keeping on top to try and get the youngest title as a example. Overall id give the game a 3/10, Unless you are a avid F1 fan, who can look past the almost fake complex mechanics to play a casual and easy management game I'd skip this. If you instead are able to look past the game needing the right names of teams I would recommend getting motorsport manager as to me its a much more rewarding, interesting and fun example of this style of game.

First impressions: Extremely polished and bug-free for an early access release. The same good ol' D**mRL action. (Let's all take a moment of silence to extend a gigantic middle finger to Bethesda/Zenimax lawyers for going after that wonderful fan project.) But the dungeon changed. I didn't encounter an equivalent of the stairs to Hell's Arena in my run, so I dunno if the dungeon is a reskin and we can expect to encounter familiar places under a new name, or if it's a complete redesign. Redesign is better I guess, to get brand new content to play, since we can still download and play DRL, which is even getting new updates thanks to this game. I know most monsters are simply reskinned from D**mRL with the same mechanics, but I find the new sprites, sound and names well-chosen. Not knowing the capacities of a new, large enemy was really scary again, good job there. Some enemies also have variants (frost, poison) which I don't remember from the predecessor game. Perks have been reworked, for instance Reloader lvl2 is more powerful than lvl1 now, and lvl 3 has the effect from the previously separate "Shottyman" perk that depended on lvl2. One major, welcome convenience is that weapons that drop from enemies are always empty of ammo. Gone is the compulsive alterning between the G (pick up) and U (unload) keys to make sure you loot every bit of ammo on the map to make sure you don't penalize yourself. This is one instance where I'll take gameplay over "realism". If you're coming to this from Jupiter Hell and not D**mRL, prepare to enjoy the various liquid floors (water, acid, lava) and the destructible walls, they add so much to the atmosphere. I have some minor gripes with the UI (such as the one for modding weapons) which takes too many clicks and keystrokes to perform some actions, and makes it hard to compare weapons properly. Also, level generation is sometimes not that great, cutting off sections behind large bodies of acid or lava, which are very expensive to cross, and placing teleporters and levers that are too dangerous to be worth trying. Eventually, you'll figure out ways to deal with it, but those situations will always drain your resources, sometimes for nothing in return. (BTW, if you never experienced the original DRL, it's free, you can download it from chaosforge, or even easier, get the DRL mod for this game from the Steam Workshop.)

It's more of Paladins VR than Overwatch VR: laggy mess with barely functional matchmaking but incredibly fun to play. Larcenauts succeeds at being a hero shooter: every class is unique and feels overpowered in its own way. Current roster has 9 heroes including archer and melee brawler. The balance is not perfect, but it's a work in progress. The gameplay is fast paced constant action: grappling points and class abilities provide fast movement while objectives discourage sitting in one place for too long. However infrequent server side lags can destroy all the fun: they range from small delays and desync to huge lag spikes that render a game unplayable for up to a minute. Shooting feels arcadey but enjoyable and there a lot of accessibility settings. I especially appreciate optional button press reloading, since Reverb G2 controllers are horrible for manual reloading. Player base is not too big for a cross-platfrom game: full 6v6 matches are only possible during peak hours. The rest of the time it will be about 3-8 players in a session with empty slots filled with bots. And AI is terrible: they can barely walk without getting stuck all the time. With small play base come issues with matchmaking: in every match experienced players will be mixed with newbies making new player experience particularly painful at times. And to add insult to injury Larcenauts matchmaking can't even distribute human players between teams equally. There are a lot of 2v4, 3v5, etc and the system doesn't bother to change team distribution between matches most of the time.

So it is situational and not very strong. For the campaign: Unlike DLC1, you don't start off with a lot to work with. You begin with an extremely crappy class with barely any skills or slots to put them in. The first mission might as well of been called "Welcome to Dark Souls", and the 2nd mission literally threw multiple Hunters at me. With the super crappy beginning class. I did some save scumming and running like crazy to get past a few missions and can't seem to unlock anything good, so it has been even less fun than DLC1. DLC3: Weapon modding. I do recommend getting this DLC if only to change the bullets of your main gun, so that it is more easy to cover armor pierce or energy stun. I've yet to do the campaign for this one, but until I update for that, just assume it is as bad as the other two or worse since that is the growing trend here. Overall: Each one adds something substantial to skirmish or multiplayer, but the campaigns are by far worse than the original.

Prismatica is a color theory puzzle game where colors are scrambled and you have to rotate the gears to move the colored tiles around until they are in their appropriate places. This includes their combinations as well (example: If a red and a yellow gear have shared tiles, those tiles will turn orange). There are four total sections, each with a standard and challenge category of 12 puzzles (so there are a total of 48 puzzles that are the same in both standard mode and challenge mode). Standard mode gives you your first of three stars for that level, and challenge mode asks you to finish the same puzzle under a certain number of moves and under a certain amount of time to get the other two stars. I finished the game with all puzzles at three stars in about 11 hours. I definitely enjoyed my time with this game. I think it's great that there is a standard and challenge mode. A nice feature they included is that you don't have to finish both of the challenges at once to get the other two stars. You can focus on one at a time if you would prefer, because once you complete a task it gives you the star. This is much more preferable to having to be conscious of the moves you are making, while still moving as quickly as possible. When it came to the challenges, I felt there were levels that gave you plenty of time/number of moves to complete it, but there were also some others that felt like it didn't give quite enough wiggle room for mistakes. I did find, however, that after moving forward in standard mode, the challenge mode for earlier levels became easier to handle because of the extra practice I had gotten, so I recommend continuing standard or just jumping to a different challenge level if you are having trouble. The game settings are pretty simple, but this isn't really an issue because of the minimalist nature of the game. There is a button to toggle music on and off and another button to toggle sound effects on and off. There is also a colorblind mode that puts symbols over the colors for clearer matching. I ended up muting sound effects because they became a bit irritating to listen to. I kept the music on because it had enough variation and I enjoyed its upbeat nature. The fanfare that comes with completing a level filled me with so much joy and satisfaction. It made working through the puzzles very rewarding. I definitely recommend this game to those who are looking for a short but fun experience that exercises your brain. I felt myself starting to understand the required rotations necessary to move the tiles where I wanted to (In that respect I very much see how the Rubik's Cube inspired them), and at the end of each level I felt accomplished and pleased. Some may feel that the price is a little high with the amount of hours played, so if that's the case go ahead and get it on a sale, but I personally enjoyed the whole experience enough to say it's worth the full price.

Other games wish they were Batman: Arkham Asylum. I'm a diehard fan of plenty of different fandoms, but nothing comes remotely close to how I feel about Batman. I love him, want to be him, and the beauty of this game is that you feel like Batman. You get into his mindset, and you become him. And it's beautiful. My first Arkham game was City, and it will forever get the nostalgia brownie points from me. I love how open the world is and how many easter eggs are hidden throughout the game. I don't know how many hours I have logged on the 360 of AC... so I will say, going into this was a bit odd, not having all the combat capabilities that you start out with in the sequel, but I was also a bit lost in it by not having the context from AA. But nothing will beat the claustrophobia of Arkham Asylum, the neverending hallways, the sleeper agent Asylum chime; the first time you get out of Intensive Treatment and onto the Island. The giant greenish moon, the constant chattering from "Warden Joker". I do prefer the plot of City, and one could argue the ending in Asylum was a bit anticlimactic in comparison but the aesthetic was perfect in Asylum. Once I replay City (again times 5) I do believe having this game under my belt will make the experience ten times better. To close, don't ask how many screenshots I took of Joker while playing through this. Just don't. I'm vengeance.

This review is mainly for those who have never played this game: Many of the reviews here will criticize the game for its many aspects. Note, that those are most likely written by veterans like myself, but without taking into consideration the viewpoint of a new player. I put the summary in the beginning: Yes, this is a dated game. Yes, the code is far from perfect. Yes, the population has declined over the years. BUT! The game's visuals aged quite well, easy to get used to it and some of the environments are really well crafted to look appealing even with dated graphics. The game has an extreme amount of content in it. Even by staying F2P ("froob" by ingame jargon) you can spend years with it. Not mandatory though, you can play this game both casually and hardcore. You decide. Microtransactions are not pay to win. There is a relatively small, but active population. In short: despite it's shortcomings AO is still the best MMORPG ever in my opion. And I have tried a few. GOLDEN TIP: FIND AN ORGANIZATION QUICKLY! (AO's jargon for Guild) Ask around in public chat channels (such as "OOC") and you will find an organization in no time. OK here come the details: Setting: AO is literally the world's first scifi MMORPG. It has a unique world that combines elements from Shadowrun (main influence), Dune and others. But it also contains many unique, sometimes humorous, sometimes quirky and sometimes outright weird aspects. The game's world is totally lovable and one of the reasons it still has an active playerbase. Fun fact: women seem to like the game world too. I have seen more women in this game (proportionally) than in any other online game. AO also has a well crafted story, which is not forced upon you if you are not into it. But if you are, there are tons of lore available, and even a novel ("Prophet without honor") There are many seasonal events, which are now part of the game's traditions and add a lot of fun. Social vs Solo: Most things in this game can be solo'ed. In fact, some of the greatest achievements are when someone is able to solo something that normally would require multiple players. You can solo almost all the way to endgame. But it is much more fun and easier to do it with other people. The game factilitates social interactions and fomations of communities and the existing communities are mostly very welcoming. I have created a couple of long-lasting real life friendships as have many other players in this game. Graphics: I won't lie: the game has aged graphics. Probably one of the least pretty MMOs that you can find on the market. But it is very easy to get used to it. The environments are well crafted, especially the Shadowlands. NOTE: there is a "new engine" game client, which is not shipped with Steam, but you can download it from the AO website. It makes the game a lot prettier, but it is still in Beta and there are a couple of bugs in it (nothing game-breaking, I play on the new client for instance) Game mechanics: It is quite similar to other online RPGs, but a lot more complex. It is mostly stat-based. The learning curve is huge, but not steep. The game will go easy on you in the beginning and you will learn it gradually. This complexity is one of the biggest appeals of this game. Equipping your character the best possible way is very challenging, but at the same time very rewarding. For instance when your low level character is able to whack high level monsters. In most cases you can adjust the difficulty of the game to your character by choosing appropriately leveled missions, or killing the appropriate level monsters in the open world. Having said that, the game has a massive open world, but also contains many instanced (somtimes even randomly generated) areas. The are unique open world bosses, open world raids, instanced raids, PVP-PVM mix raids and many others Professions (the game's equivalent of character classes) are wildly different and unique in their own way. BUT most items are not class locked, and there is a big room for experimentation. You are not really forced a certain path like in other games, say in SWTOR where if you are a smuggler you must use blasters. In AO blasters would be the recommended choice, but it can happen that someone comes up with a creative setup that outperforms the recommended one. The variety options are immense. PVP in this game is the "smartest" pvp I have seen in any game. It takes a lot of skill and game knowledge to be at the top, but the entry level is not that scary. I reiterate though: you do not need to be knowledgeable to get started. It will come both naturally, and the community will answer your questions. Your organization members will lend their deep game knowledge to you and will help you along the way to stand on your own feet, if you need it. Microtransactions: Completely optional. Most players get by without ever spending money on microtransactions. On the other hand it's a good way to support the developers. Membership: Around 50% of the content is tied to a subscription plan. It is farily affordable, but more expensive than pretty much any other MMO on the market. Bummer, a dated business model. As a F2P player, you will have access to "Rubi-Ka", the main world of the game. Subscription players gain access to the "Shadowlands" which presents an alternative progression (ie. you can level both in Rubi-Ka and the Shadowlands) which is arguably faster in the Shadowlands. You will get acces to more endgame content too. More powerful items etc. You can choose to play the full game from day one, or remain a free player as long as you want. Many of the subscription players today started out as F2P players, and there are some players who still play F2P accounts after so many years. Complaints, negative reviews, vitriolic statements from veterans: AO runs on minimal support from it's developer company. This makes the game somewhat riddled with problems. You will hear a lot about exploiters, broken economy, inflation etc. None of them are exactly true, though none of them are false either. Very rarely it happens that a small group of exploiters pop up. Since AO does not have constant supervision, these are not addressed promptly. Still the holes are plugged and the "outbreak" itself does not have much effect on the game anyway (not even close to what many veterans would tell you - they usually see this problem being a lot larger than it really is). Also, despite what anyone says, the economy is not (that) broken. It will not affect your gameplay much anyway. It will not prevent you from having fun or getting what you need on your character. TL;DR : AO is a big, complex, lovable game. Nowhere near perfect, but its pros outweigh the cons in my opinion. A must try. Stick to it. FIND A GUILD!

Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened is a full remake of the 2007 title by Frogwares, rebuilt from the ground up in Unreal Engine 4. It’s both a detective adventure and a Lovecraftian horror story, blending Arthur Conan Doyle’s iconic characters with the cosmic dread of H.P. Lovecraft. The game serves as a continuation of Sherlock Holmes: Chapter One, exploring Holmes’ early career alongside Dr. Watson. The narrative begins as a standard Holmes mystery in Victorian London, but it quickly spirals into something darker. Holmes and Watson investigate a series of kidnappings, uncovering a sinister cult obsessed with the Great Old Ones. The writing walks a fine line between classic detective storytelling and supernatural horror. Holmes is portrayed as brilliant but haunted, struggling with doubt and obsession. Watson acts as both partner and anchor, grounding the story. The Lovecraftian themes are eerie but not overly grotesque, leaning more into psychological tension than gore. Players collect clues, analyze evidence, interrogate suspects, and use Holmes’ deduction board to piece together solutions. Environments range from London streets to Louisiana swamps and Swiss asylums, each atmospheric and unsettling. The game relies on logic puzzles, observation, and connecting evidence rather than combat. Holmes’ mind can fracture under the weight of the horrors he uncovers, adding tension to the investigations. The Unreal Engine remake gives the game detailed environments and improved character models, though animations can feel stiff at times. Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened is a compelling detective adventure that successfully blends classic mystery with cosmic horror. While not flawless in execution, it delivers an immersive story, strong atmosphere, and a fresh take on Holmes’ early years. For fans of Sherlock, Lovecraft, or narrative-driven mysteries, it’s a rewarding experience. 8/10 DISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | GREAT |AMAZING| MASTERPIECE Reviewed on: Win11 Home 64-bit, Intel i5-11600K, GeForce RTX 3060 Ti 8GB TUF, 32GB DDR4-3600 RAM, 2 x Kingston NV1 1TB M.2 NVMe SSD, Internet Broadband 1000/1000 Mbit If you like this review, then please consider giving it a thumbs up. Strange Horticulture is an exquisitely crafted puzzle and exploration game that invites players into a world where botany meets mystery and folklore. Developed with an evident passion for plants and storytelling, the game offers a deeply atmospheric experience centered around running a curious herb shop in a remote and eerie village. From the moment you step into the shoes of the shopkeeper, Strange Horticulture weaves together the delicate art of plant identification with a compelling narrative that unfolds through cryptic requests, ancient secrets, and supernatural undertones. For players who enjoy slow-burning mysteries, detailed research mechanics, and atmospheric world-building, this game offers a unique and memorable adventure. At its heart, Strange Horticulture tasks players with running an old plant shop where villagers come seeking rare and sometimes bizarre herbs for their ailments or needs. The gameplay revolves around careful observation and deduction: you must examine the physical descriptions and symptoms provided by customers, then match these clues to an ever-growing compendium of plants. This process is intellectually engaging, requiring players to study botanical illustrations, cross-reference characteristics, and make informed decisions under subtle time pressure. Unlike many traditional puzzle games, Strange Horticulture rewards patience and curiosity, allowing you to gradually build knowledge rather than rush through challenges. One of the standout features of the game is its beautifully detailed plant database, which functions as both a tool and a narrative device. Each plant entry is meticulously designed, featuring hand-drawn artwork, botanical descriptions, historical uses, and notes on folklore and mythology. This encyclopedic approach immerses players in a rich world where plants carry meaning beyond their physical properties—some hold mystical powers, others are tied to local legends, and many possess symbolic weight in the unfolding story. The research element feels authentic and satisfying, giving the player a genuine sense of discovery akin to being a scholar or apothecary. The narrative in Strange Horticulture is subtle and layered, revealed gradually through the interactions with villagers, hidden notes, and the enigmatic mysteries surrounding the shop and its surroundings. The game cleverly intertwines folklore and horror, creating an unsettling atmosphere that lingers beneath the surface of its pastoral setting. Each customer’s request and story peel back another layer of the village’s secrets, encouraging players to pay close attention to dialogue and environmental cues. The story doesn’t rely on bombastic twists but rather builds tension through implication and the eerie connections between people and plants, making for an immersive and thought-provoking experience. Visually, the game is a triumph of minimalist design paired with intricate detail. The art style employs muted, earthy tones and finely drawn illustrations that evoke old botanical manuscripts and Victorian-era herbals. This aesthetic choice not only suits the game’s thematic focus but also enhances the mood of quiet mystery and antiquarian charm. The shop interface is clean and intuitive, allowing easy access to plant specimens, notes, and customer requests without overwhelming the player. Subtle animations and environmental details, such as rustling leaves or flickering candlelight, contribute to the ambiance without distracting from the core gameplay. Sound design plays a crucial role in building Strange Horticulture’s immersive atmosphere. The soundtrack consists of gentle, ambient melodies interspersed with natural sounds like wind, birdsong, and distant footsteps, all combining to create a serene yet slightly unsettling backdrop. Audio cues guide players through interactions and heighten moments of revelation or tension.
